documents.abstract: The article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations of the development of specialized marketing research methods in the context of digital economic transformation. It is substantiated that modern marketing research is undergoing profound changes associated with the transition to data-driven approaches based on the use of Big Data technologies, artificial intelligence, and machine learning. It is determined that the digitalization of marketing research contributes to increasing the accuracy of analytical results, reducing information processing time, and creating conditions for predictive and prescriptive modeling of market processes. The study reveals the features of transforming traditional research methods through their integration with digital tools, which ensures the formation of a comprehensive analytical system. The feasibility of using hybrid approaches combining qualitative and quantitative methods with modern digital technologies is proven, allowing for improved validity and representativeness of research results. The impact of digital marketing research on key business performance indicators is analyzed, including conversion rates, customer loyalty, marketing efficiency, and decision-making speed. The main limitations of digital methods are identified, such as data quality issues, algorithmic bias, and the complexity of interpreting analytical results. The necessity of forming an integrated model of marketing research is substantiated, taking into account the specifics of the digital environment and ensuring the effectiveness of analytical activities in conditions of dynamic market changes. The generalization of the obtained results allowed forming the methodological foundations for choosing optimal marketing research tools depending on the goals, conditions, and resource constraints of the enterprise. It is proven that the most effective is an integrated research model based on the synergy of analytical technologies and classical approaches to data collection. Future scientific research should be directed towards deepening the methodology of integrating artificial intelligence into marketing research, particularly regarding the development of adaptive algorithms for analyzing behavioral data.

Frontier LLM agents have been shown to be capable of solving increasingly complex tasks for which humans have measurable solutions. This begs the pertinent question of whether LLM agents can go beyond what humans have already solved. The ability to develop sophisticated strategies to tackle consequential problems becomes paramount as well-trodden, human-developed solutions become insufficient for problems for which we lack context or enough training data. We study agents' capability of such strategy formation through the communal practice of video game speedrunning. In speedrunning, practitioners compete to find the fastest way to complete a video game under certain conditions, and in so doing uncovering interesting unorthodox play styles that require a thorough understanding and mastery of the underlying game mechanics. We introduce SPEEDRUNBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates frontier LLM agents across 9 different games. To perform well in this benchmark, agents must repeatedly improve their strategy, reflect on their performance, exploit their gained knowledge, and reason across a long-horizon of actions to improve on an increasingly difficult problem: being faster than themselves and everyone else. Our experiments show that while frontier agents approach human world records in simple platformer games, they remain behind human performance on longer, more complex games under practical budgets. These results suggest that SPEEDRUNBENCH is a useful testbed for studying agents' strategy formation capabilities as well as being a saturation-resistant evaluation measure, as there is almost always a faster completion time waiting to be discovered.

Nigeria faces a convergence of severe environmental crises, including advancing desertification in the north, persistent oil pollution in the Niger Delta, and deadly farmer herder conflicts intensified by climate change and shrinking natural resources. This article argues that these challenges are not merely economic or political but are fundamentally moral and spiritual, requiring a robust theological response from the Nigerian church. Employing a newly developed framework, the Creation Mandate Stewardship Theory (CMST), grounded in the Genesis mandate and enriched by African theological insights from scholars such as Mbiti and Bediako, the study examines human responsibility toward creation through three pillars: divine ownership, relational responsibility, and accountable action. Adopting a church-historical lens, the article traces the Nigerian church's trajectory from missionary-era neglect of ecological concerns through a period of prosperity-focused silence during Nigeria's most intense years of environmental exploitation to emerging but uneven engagement with creation care in contemporary mainline denominations. Biblical foundations and African ecotheological perspectives, including the contributions of Oduyoye and Kunhiyop, are presented as resources for reframing environmental stewardship as intrinsic to Christian mission rather than a foreign import. The article further explores artificial intelligence as an emerging tool for climate monitoring, agricultural extension, conflict mitigation, and multilingual environmental education while cautioning that technology must remain subordinate to theological conviction and community trust. Institutional, economic, theological, and technological barriers to church-led environmental action are identified. The article concludes with concrete recommendations for denominations, seminaries, and policymakers, urging the Nigerian church to embrace its calling as a steward, not owner, of creation and to become an active agent of ecological healing and social peace.

This article examines how hybrid work can strengthen employee well-being and public financial management (PFM) in Birgunj Metropolitan City. Design/methodology: It uses a qualitative case-study synthesis of municipal PFM materials, remote-work survey findings, municipal documents, audit evidence and relevant literature. Findings: Flexible work can reduce commuting pressure and support continuity, but isolation, weak work–life boundaries and inadequate home workstations may undermine staff well-being. The remote-work evidence shows favourable overall quality of life (M=4.45/6), alongside limited social interaction (M=4.26), weaker colleague connection (M=4.25) and difficulty separating work from personal life (M=3.92). For PFM, digital and hybrid workflows can improve revenue administration, reconciliation, procurement tracking, reporting and transparency; however, weak controls, fragmented records and limited digital capability can reproduce existing governance failures online. Practical implications: Birgunj should introduce role-based hybrid work, secure digital systems, measurable outputs, ergonomic support and risk-based internal audit. Originality/value: The article integrates employee well-being with municipal financial governance, two themes commonly treated separately. It argues that hybrid work should be assessed not as an employee benefit alone, but as a governance intervention whose success depends on the interaction between people, processes, technology and accountability.

The rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education and the resulting institutional responses have prompted research to support evidence-based policy decisions. As policies change to adjust to this disruptive technology, it demands agility from educators. The impacts of these policy changes on student behaviours and outcomes are currently poorly understood. This study examines how students used GenAI across three assessments in an undergraduate physics unit after assessment redesign forced by institutional policy that permitted purpose-specific and open use. Using a mixed-methods approach, student declarations of GenAI use were coded into four functional categories and mapped to the Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, and Redefinition (SAMR) framework. Learning and Formatting dominated early use and aligned with substitution and augmentation for a presentation assessment type. Later assessments showed a marked growth in Feedback uses, which spanned all SAMR levels and became the most common pattern. ‘Doing Task’ uses appeared in smaller numbers but illustrated modification and redefinition when GenAI generated step-by-step solutions for unfamiliar problems. Across all assessments, GenAI users achieved slightly higher scores, although differences were not statistically significant, so this trend should be interpreted as a tentative observation. Findings suggest that assessment design, which rewards understanding and requires student judgement, aligns with the theoretical markers of evaluative judgement. While this study did not directly measure internal cognitive states, the observed change in functional behaviour, specifically the transition toward iterative feedback loops, suggests that GenAI could serve as a catalyst for learning. This study provides empirical evidence on how assessment redesign based on policy shifts influences GenAI use patterns and proposes design principles for authentic assessment in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) contexts. It highlights authentic assessment and constructive alignment as guiding principles for sustainable policy and pedagogy in the GenAI era, ensuring coherence among learning outcomes, activities, and assessment.

Background Interpreters work under substantial cognitive, emotional, physical, and organizational demands, yet evidence on the resources supporting their wellbeing and professional functioning remains dispersed across settings and modalities. This study developed and prioritized a multilevel support framework through expert consensus. Methods A literature-informed framework comprising four dimensions and 31 candidate sub-themes was developed through a targeted narrative review, thematic synthesis, and content and face review. Of 20 experts invited, 15 completed an online questionnaire using a seven-point importance scale. Ratings were analyzed using the Fuzzy Delphi Method according to predefined consensus and retention criteria. Results All four dimensions and 27 candidate sub-themes met the retention criteria, yielding a sub-theme retention rate of 87.10%. Within the expert panel, professional preparedness, agency, and sustainable competence received the strongest dimension-level endorsement ( A = 0.838). Organizational, employment, and occupational health support ranked fourth at the dimension level ( A = 0.693), yet contained the most strongly endorsed candidate overall, manageable workload, scheduling, breaks, recovery time, and assignment rotation ( A = 0.902). This was followed by two D2 candidates: assignment-specific contextual and terminological preparation ( A = 0.860) and decision latitude ( A = 0.833). Four candidates fell below the expert-agreement criterion (60.00%−73.33%): trauma- and emotion-informed interpreting competence, inclusion as a member of the service team, confidential professional supervision, and acoustic and hearing safety. Each satisfied the mean-threshold and defuzzification criteria. They were thus excluded from the proposed cross-context core and warrant context-specific reassessment. Conclusion The resulting panel-endorsed content framework advances a multilevel conceptualization of individual, professional, relational, and organizational resources and provides a structured basis for interpreter education, professional support, organizational policy, and occupational-health planning. While the rankings are confined to the relative priorities of this 15-member panel and provide no basis for a universal or causal hierarchy, the framework offers a foundation for subsequent measurement, validation, and implementation research involving more diverse panels across interpreting settings and modalities.

The drive toward sustainable supply chain management (SSCM) in Africa is gaining momentum as nations strive to reconcile economic development with environmental stewardship and social inclusivity. The advent of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) – marked by the integration of technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, internet of things (IoT), and big data analytics – presents a double-edged sword for African economies: significant opportunities to transform supply chains sustainably, yet also formidable challenges stemming from infrastructural, technological, and institutional deficits. Despite weak transport networks, limited digital infrastructure, and regulatory inefficiencies, African countries are increasingly exploring how 4IR tools can address systemic inefficiencies, improve transparency, and promote ethical and environmentally responsible sourcing practices. This chapter examines how Industry 4.0 (I4.0) can serve as a catalyst for sustainable supply chains in Africa by optimizing logistics, reducing waste, improving product traceability, and enabling data-driven decision-making. It highlights the transformative potential of technologies like blockchain for traceability, AI for predictive analytics, and green innovations like renewable energy-powered logistics. Nevertheless, implementation barriers – including digital illiteracy, cyber vulnerabilities, and the skills gap – remain significant. The study emphasizes the importance of localized technology adoption, policy support, and investment in human capital to fully realize SSCM goals. It concludes that with strategic integration of 4IR technologies and regional cooperation, African nations can build resilient and competitive supply chains aligned with the sustainable development goals (SDGs) and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) vision.

documents.abstract: Abstract Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent organic pollutants with widespread environmental occurrence. Their toxicity and resistance to degradation pose serious risks to ecosystems and human health. While existing separation (e.g., adsorption, filtration) and degradation (e.g., photochemical, electrochemical, thermal) technologies can achieve partial PFAS removal, limitations such as high energy demand, poor cost-efficiency, and harsh operating conditions hinder their in situ application. In this context, a synergistic approach, a system in which adsorption and degradation are functionally coupled rather than applied as independent sequential unit operations, has emerged as a promising route. This review critically examines the coupling of biopolymer-based adsorption and photocatalytic degradation as a sustainable and effective solution for PFAS remediation. Biopolymers such as lignin, chitosan, and cellulose offer a renewable alternative to conventional sorbents, exhibiting adsorption capacities of ∼50–500 mg g–1 and beyond in advanced systems and removal efficiencies of up to 99% in dilute conditions, while photocatalytic platforms, such as semiconductor-based systems, reach ∼32–100% degradation efficiencies, with up to 92% defluorination in optimized systems. When combined functionally, these systems enhance PFAS degradation through interfacial preconcentration and reduce secondary waste. The review critically evaluates recent advances in material development, mechanistic understanding, and system integration, alongside the roles of Life Cycle Assessment and Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning, as complementary tools guiding the design and deployment of sustainable PFAS-remediation strategies.

Nghiên cứu đề xuất và thử nghiệm quy trình tạo sinh tự động câu hỏi trắc nghiệm khách quan (TNKQ) tiếng Việt dựa trên mô hình ngôn ngữ lớn (LLM), trong đó mỗi câu hỏi được gắn với một chuẩn đầu ra học phần (Course Learning Outcomes - CLO) và một mức nhận thức theo thang Bloom cải tiến, đồng thời được dựa vào nội dung giáo trình bằng kỹ thuật truy xuất BM25 nhằm hạn chế hiện tượng ảo giác nội dung. Khác với các nghiên cứu trước dựa vào giảng viên đánh giá thủ công hoặc dùng một LLM tự đánh giá bản thân, nghiên cứu này đề xuất cơ chế chấm chéo giữa hai LLM thuộc hai họ độc lập (LLaMA-3.3-70B và Qwen3-32B) làm phương pháp đánh giá tự động. Thử nghiệm trên học phần Mạng và truyền thông với 40 câu hỏi sinh được cho thấy hệ thống đạt mức đồng thuận đáp án tốt đến rất tốt (Cohen's κ = 0,78–0,82) và độ bám sát giáo trình rất cao (0,97–0,99), nhưng bộc lộ thách thức lớn khi phân loại mức nhận thức Bloom (κ = 0,03–0,26). Kết quả khẳng định xu hướng khả thi của AI trong hỗ trợ đánh giá đại học, đồng thời chỉ rõ ranh giới giữa năng lực tự động hóa và vai trò không thể thay thế của giảng viên.

This chapter examines the transformation of teaching and learning in the digital university as a gradual, uneven, and institutionally embedded process rather than as a simple technological upgrade. The contemporary university increasingly depends on learning management systems, artificial intelligence, learning analytics, digital communication platforms, immersive environments, and modular credentials. These tools reshape the organisation of courses, the experience of students, the work of academic teachers, and the governance of educational quality. Drawing on constructivist approaches to learning, cognitive load theory, critical digital pedagogy, and debates on educational governance, the chapter discusses both the pedagogical potential and the institutional risks of digitalisation. It argues that digital technologies can support personalisation, accessibility, flexible participation, and the diversification of learning pathways, but only when they are embedded in thoughtful instructional design and accompanied by adequate institutional support. At the same time, the chapter draws attention to the risks associated with excessive dependence on platform infrastructures, automated assessment, predictive analytics, surveillance-oriented systems, and market-driven models of educational provision. Particular attention is paid to the digital divide, accessibility, academic integrity in the context of generative AI, and the need to preserve mentorship, academic freedom, intellectual curiosity, and interpersonal dialogue. The chapter concludes that the future of digital higher education should not be framed as a choice between technology and humanistic academic values. Rather, the central task is to develop pedagogically responsible, ethically governed, and socially inclusive digital learning environments in which technologies extend the human purposes of higher education instead of replacing them.

# TeleTwin: Code, Data and Results Release accompanying the paper **"TeleTwin: A Calibrated Digital Twin of TelegramCrisis Discourse as a Ground-Truth Testbed for Detecting LLM-Powered InformationOperations"** by Despoina Antonakaki and Sotiris Ioannidis (FORTH-ICS, TechnicalUniversity of Crete). TeleTwin is an LLM-powered digital twin of a Telegram ecosystem discussing theIsrael–Gaza and Iran–Israel conflict (March–August 2025). Channels are the agents;each simulated channel is instantiated from the calibration-period posts of a realchannel. The twin is evaluated on a held-out period containing the June 2025Iran–Israel war (RQ1). It is then used, together with the real data, as a testbedfor detecting LLM-powered coordinated campaigns (RQ2). ## Contents ```code/ collection, calibration, simulation, baselines, detectors, evaluationconfig/ crawl.yaml (sampling frame, keywords); campaigns_public.yaml (campaign design factors; narrative texts withheld)data/ channels.csv 204 channels in the frame: id, username, title, subscribers, sampling stage, discovery path, perspective label, state affiliation (reviewed by the authors) perspective_labels.csv perspective labels with confidence and notes messages_metadata.csv.gz 1,074,018 messages (1 Mar – 31 Aug 2025) WITHOUT text: ids, dates, forward links (source channel + original message), views, forwards, replies, reactions, media type, topic tags (Gaza/Iran, Ukraine) twin_agents.json / twin_agents_v2.json / twin_wires.json agent and wire profiles (calibration statistics; style- example texts removed) campaign_labels_tierA.csv.gz ground truth of the synthetic campaigns: campaign, replicate seed, campaign channel (negative id), message kind (narrative/cover), narrative id, timestamp, donor channel whose voice was borrowed (no text)results/ calibration/ per-channel and ecosystem statistics, calibration vs held-out period rq1/ fidelity metrics per run (TeleTwin v1/v2, static and reactive baselines) rq2/ Tier A (campaigns in real data) and Tier B (campaigns in the twin) detection and diffusion results tuning_runs.md simulator calibration history corpus_stats.json, search_candidates*.json, balance_excluded.json``` ## Reproducing the pipeline Python 3.10+, `telethon`, `pyyaml`, `httpx`, `numpy`, `scipy`, `scikit-learn`,`sentence-transformers`; an OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint (we used vLLM servingQwen2.5-72B-Instruct-AWQ on one NVIDIA H200). 1. `collect_ecosystem.py --mode discover | expand | search | backfill` — sampling frame and full channel timelines (needs Telegram API credentials). Message texts can be re-hydrated from `messages_metadata.csv.gz` with the Telegram API, subject to availability of the original posts.2. `perspective_labels.py`, `calibration_stats.py`, `corpus_stats.py` — labels and statistics.3. `build_agents.py [--examples proportional]` — agent and wire profiles (calibration period only).4. `simulate.py --start --end --run [--agents] [--seed] [--campaign --embed]` — the twin.5. `baseline.py --mode static|reactive` — non-LLM null models.6. `eval_rq1.py`, `eval_rq2.py`, `eval_tierB.py` with `detectors.py` — evaluation. ## What is withheld, and why Following the paper's Ethics section, this release does **not** contain:- message texts of real channels (only identifiers and metadata);- simulated message texts, which are generated in the voice of real channels;- the texts of the campaign narratives and the prompts and code used to generate campaign content (`campaigns.py`). All narratives are fictional; the generator is withheld to avoid releasing a ready-made tool for producing coordinated content. It is available to researchers on request for verification purposes. No information about Telegram users or subscribers was collected; all data concernpublic broadcast channels. ## Licence Code: MIT. Data and results: CC BY 4.0. See `LICENSE`. ## Citation Antonakaki, D. and Ioannidis, S. (2026). TeleTwin: A Calibrated Digital Twin ofTelegram Crisis Discourse as a Ground-Truth Testbed for Detecting LLM-PoweredInformation Operations. The Internet is shifting from a human-centric web towards an agentic frontier, with artificial intelligence (AI) agents increasingly integrated into daily life. The transition from instruction-based bots to goal-orientated agents is accelerating, signalling a move from automation to autonomy. According to internal Akamai data, AI bot traffic grew by 300 per cent over the past year, bringing a new kind of Internet traffic characterised by distinct behaviours. As AI agents evolve, existing security defences are proving inadequate; signature-based rules cannot effectively counter reasoning-driven agents. This paper examines the taxonomy of attacks, both AI as a threat and threats targeting AI systems. Whether dealing with aggressive AI inference crawlers such as Bytespider or innovative AI-engineered threats, current security limitations heighten business risks and operational challenges. This necessitates a fundamental evolution, not only of traditional firewalls but also of the security architecture, towards a new, agent-aware defence framework that moves beyond identifying who is accessing resources to understanding the intent and logic of autonomous actors. Semantic firewalls are essential, protecting users and agents at input and output stages while keeping models safe. To enable verifiable autonomy, strategic shifts at the board level are critical, establishing governance frameworks that allow organisations to transition from black-box models to transparent, verifiable glass-box models, paving the way for trustworthy autonomous systems. This article is also included in The Business & Management Collection which can be accessed at https://hstalks.com/business/.

Multi-framework Governance, Risk and Compliance (GRC) platforms increasingly automate the link between an organisation's self-assessment answer and the compliance obligations that answer is said to satisfy. Cross-framework control mapping, AI-suggested question correlation, and automatic propagation of answers and evidence across correlated questions all serve the legitimate efficiency goal of reducing duplicate work for small and medium-sized enterprises under the EU Cyber Resilience Act, NIS2 and GDPR. The same mechanisms, however, amplify the consequences of any human-factor bias in a single answer: one optimistically-graded control, one rubber-stamped attestation, or one AI-drafted answer can be silently replicated as evidence of compliance with many obligations across multiple frameworks. We call this the amplifier effect: a platform-design property (coarse-grained attestation and un-gated propagation) rather than a failing of individual users. Using two EU-funded SME-facing GRC platforms, CYBERFORT and CYBER-BRIDGE, as examples, we (i) describe the amplification mechanism in concrete data-model terms, (ii) propose a six-dimension scoring framework for evaluating any GRC tool's exposure to the effect, (iii) instantiate the framework on a thirteen-tool comparison covering enterprise IRM, mid-market platforms, compliance-automation tools, and the two EU SME projects, and (iv) outline a measurement protocol that a consortium with access to production self-assessment data can run. The thirteen-tool comparison is a structured design assessment, not an empirical measurement of user behaviour. The EU SME platforms score lowest on the amplifier dimensions because their burden-reduction design deliberately trades sign-off granularity for throughput; we report this as a design trade-off, not a verdict on the platforms. Our contribution is the framing and the measurement protocol.

This article examines the potential application of generative artificial intelligence in the visual communication of Almaty’s city brand. The study aims to identify the city’s principal visual resources, analyze existing communication challenges, and determine the prospects for using AI in the creation and adaptation of city-brand content. The key elements of Almaty’s identity include the mountain landscape of the Trans-Ili Alatau, apple-related symbolism, Kazakh cultural motifs, Soviet-era architectural heritage, green public spaces, and the contemporary creative environment. The analysis shows that the fragmented visual representation of the city reduces its recognizability and weakens brand coherence. Generative AI can accelerate the development of visual concepts, support multilingual communication, and facilitate the adaptation of materials for different target audiences. However, its use also involves risks of cultural inaccuracy, stylistic homogenization, copyright infringement, and the loss of local authenticity. The article proposes a human-AI collaborative model based on expert review, audience evaluation, and final human control.

This conceptual paper introduces the CARE Framework for Situated Ethical Deliberation, a practice-oriented approach for evaluating specific uses of artificial intelligence in healthcare, behavioral health, social work, human services, and related professional settings. CARE organizes ethical deliberation around four interdependent dimensions: Context, Authority, Risk, and Engagement. Rather than treating an AI system as the sole unit of analysis, the framework examines a bounded use within a particular setting—including the people affected, the purpose of the technology, the authority assigned to it, the potential distribution of harms and benefits, and the role of meaningful human participation and relationships. The framework supports transparent, case-specific decisions about whether an AI use should proceed as proposed, proceed with safeguards, be narrowed or piloted, undergo additional review, be paused, be declined, or be discontinued. Contrasting practice scenarios demonstrate how ethical judgments may change when an AI system’s function, authority, context, consequences, or relational significance changes. CARE is presented as a conceptually grounded, practice-informed framework intended to complement—not replace—professional standards, technical validation, organizational governance, legal requirements, or discipline-specific review. It is offered for scholarly critique, professional application, refinement, and future empirical evaluation.

documents.abstract: Healthcare system is a major issue facing many backlashes across the world. It faces several issues and challenges like the cost and growing health diseases, uneven access to the system, shortage of staffs and support, and the burden of excessive chronic diseases across the world. Although healthcare system has many data which can be used in many ways, they unfortunately remain unused or are ignored. However, there is an invention or a new pathway called artificial intelligence (AI) that has enabled using all the data for clinical system&s;s decisions and automation of tasks. This chapter throws light on the current situation of healthcare sector and how AI can transform the industry in a better and useful way. It discusses many processes like medical imaging, analytics prediction, customised medicine, discovery of drugs, and many more. The advantages of AI include quicker and more accurate results, improved efficiency, cost-cutting, and smoother patient experiences. However, many challenges remain like issues of data privacy, biasness, transparency, and regulation and integration into workflows in clinic. Ethical considerations and policymaking are essential to ensure safety and fair use of AI. AI is not a replacement or take away of anyone&s;s job but a powerful and helpful partner that can help in decision-making, improve access, and upgrade the healthcare systems when implemented wisely and accurately.

documents.abstract: Abstract How do humans perceive and evaluate creativity when it is attributed to artificial intelligence (AI)? This research examined how labeling a source as “AI” versus “human” systematically biases creativity evaluations across different domains. In experiment 1 (painting and poetry), outputs labeled as human-created were rated as more creative than identical AI-labeled outputs in artistic creation. Experiment 2, which manipulated the attribution of co-created works, revealed that the “human ideation with AI assistance” label enhanced perceived originality in poetry, whereas those attributed primarily to humans remained dominant in evaluations of painting. Experiment 3 utilized a divergent thinking task (Alternative Uses Test), found a reversal: the same output received higher creativity ratings when bearing an AI label. The findings reveal a domain-specific pattern in attitudes toward AI creativity: viewing collaboration positively yet maintaining a persistent bias in valuing AI’s creative contributions.

Artificial intelligence increasingly shapes how e-commerce platforms recommend integrated financial services, yet evidence concerning Generation X remains limited. This methodological study examines the relationships among perceived AI-based recommendation quality, trust, and embedded finance use, while also distinguishing recommendation quality from exposure frequency. A structured synthetic dataset of 300 observations representing Generation X e-commerce users in Jakarta was analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling with 10,000 bootstrap subsamples. AI-based recommendations were positively related to embedded finance use (β = 0.514) and trust (β = 0.444), while trust was positively related to use (β = 0.240); all paths had p < 0.001. The indirect effect through trust was significant (β = 0.107), indicating complementary partial mediation, and the model explained 43.1% of the variance in use. A contextual cross-tabulation showed that recommendation exposure frequency was not associated with purchase response (p = 0.818). The study's novelty lies in showing that, for digitally experienced Generation X profiles, perceived relevance and accuracy matter more than repeated exposure, while trust strengthens but does not dominate the relationship. Empirical validation with linked respondent-level data remains necessary.

Generative artificial intelligence offers new opportunities to support higher-order thinking in elementary education, yet empirical evidence of its effectiveness remains limited. This study examined the effectiveness of ChatGPT-assisted inquiry learning in improving critical thinking skills among fifth-grade students in science learning. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control-group design involved 60 students assigned to an experimental group (n = 30) and a control group (n = 30). The experimental group received four weeks of teacher-guided ChatGPT-assisted inquiry learning, while the control group received conventional instruction. Critical thinking skills were assessed before and after the intervention using a validated structured essay test. The groups had comparable baseline scores (58.43 ± 8.71 vs. 57.86 ± 8.24; p = 0.781). After the intervention, the experimental group achieved significantly higher critical thinking scores than the control group (84.76 ± 6.25 vs. 67.91 ± 7.42), with a mean difference of 16.85 points (95% CI: 13.21–20.49; p < 0.001) and a large effect size (Cohen’s d = 1.92). The greatest improvements were observed in analysis and evaluation. These findings demonstrate that teacher-guided ChatGPT-assisted inquiry learning can effectively enhance elementary students’ critical thinking skills. Its classroom implementation should emphasize structured inquiry and teacher supervision to promote responsible use of generative AI. Future studies should examine its long-term effects across larger and more diverse elementary school populations and investigate its effectiveness across different subjects and learning contexts.

The role of the researcher is rapidly evolving as LLMs and coding agents become part of everyday scientific workflows, shifting the work from writing code towards verifying it. The role of the research software engineer is shifting with it. In this talk we draw on our experience as research software engineers at the Bristol Centre for Supercomputing, home to Isambard-AI and part of the UK's AI Research Resource (AIRR), looking at this shift from the perspective of both the engineer and the infrastructure provider. As users increasingly turn to these tools, we discuss what it takes to support them, and what that means for research in heliophysics and UK space science more broadly.

This paper responds to Anthropic's September 29, 2026 “What Do You Want From AI?” public consultation from the perspective of the Generative Agency Protocol (GAP), a human-centered framework concerned with preserving Meaningful Human Agency and human cognitive, agentic, and normative sovereignty during sustained Human–AI interaction. It argues for Human Alignment as a governing orientation for AI development and introduces several GAP concepts relevant to the consultation, including the GAP Trichotomy, Human Sovereignty, Triune Interpretability, HAI Longitudinalism, HAI Longitudinal Human Exigency, and the AI Trolley Scenario.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

The chapter examines the effects of digitalization and artificial intelligence (AI) on human experience, understanding and healing. It compares the associated developments with the three major historical blows to humanity caused by scientific discoveries: the Copernican revolution, Darwin&s;s theory of evolution, and Freud&s;s discovery of the unconscious. The changes in our sense of self and identity under the influence of digital technologies are discussed, as are the resulting challenges for psychotherapy. In this context, the current trend toward self-construction and the increasing desensualization are critically examined. The author shows how this trend is changing human coexistence and the relationship between people and their environment. In particular, he traces the current developments surrounding AI and their impact on education, ethical issues and, last but not least, psychotherapy. For example, emotional robotics and virtual reality are presented with regard to their possible use in a psychotherapeutic setting, and the associated opportunities and risks for Bioenergetic Analysis are explained.

documents.abstract: Research on teachers and generative artificial intelligence has largely measured how much they use these tools, leaving open which cognitive operations they hand over. We asked whether the layer of processing delegated during lesson preparation predicts what happens in the classroom. Ninety junior secondary mathematics teachers in 18 public schools in eastern China were followed across four waves of video-recorded lessons over one school year, yielding 897 coded lessons, 4,640 unplanned student contributions, 1,518 preparation sessions, and 556 stimulated-recall interviews. For each lesson, the final plan was compared against the interaction logs segment by segment, producing two ratios that index offloading by provenance: generative-layer offloading, the share of questioning and variation segments originating in model output, and formulation-layer offloading, the share of context and wording segments. Three-level models decomposing within- and between-teacher variation showed that the two layers behaved differently. Within teachers, generative-layer offloading was associated with less higher-order questioning, less substantive uptake of student talk, weaker maintenance of high cognitive demand, and lower recognition and substantive use of unplanned student contributions, with standardized coefficients between 0.08 and 0.18. Formulation-layer offloading was unrelated to four of those indicators, positively associated with the length and variety of designed variation sequences, and positively associated with recognition of unplanned contributions, the single indicator on which the two layers cross in opposite directions. Total preparation time with AI predicted discourse outcomes on its own and lost that value for the lesson-level indicators once layer composition was entered. An embedded micro-randomized comparison, in which teachers drafted their own questioning and variation sequence before consulting the model, lowered generative-layer offloading and raised substantive uptake. Professional attention to student thinking, coded from stimulated-recall interviews conducted after the lesson by a separate team, followed the same within-teacher pattern and carried the association with the substantive use of unplanned contributions. However, the retrospective measurement leaves its direction open. Teachers’ post-preparation confidence rose with generative-layer offloading by 0.23 standard deviations per within-teacher standard deviation. It carried no positive information about the lesson that followed, a confidence-performance dissociation. What predicted classroom discourse was which layer was delegated, not how much.

documents.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Conventional binostril endoscopic endonasal approaches (EEAs) provide optimal surgical ergonomics but are often associated with sinonasal morbidity. Conversely, mononostril approaches preserve mucosal integrity at the expense of surgical maneuverability. We hypothesized that the modified sparing binostril approach (moSBA) may provide a favorable balance between surgical exposure, ergonomics, and sinonasal preservation while maintaining flexibility for risk-adapted reconstruction. This study evaluates the feasibility and functional outcomes of this technique combined with a risk-adapted skull base reconstruction strategy. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 81 patients who underwent EEA or extended EEA for sellar and suprasellar lesions between 2021 and 2025. All procedures were performed combining a paraseptal and a contralateral endonasal corridor (moSBA). The risk-adapted reconstructive algorithm included type 1 (hemostatic material with free mucosal graft), type 2 (inlay fat graft with onlay nasoseptal flap), and type 3 (modified gasket-seal). Outcomes included extent of resection, complications, and 22-item Sinonasal Outcome Test (SNOT-22) assessment. RESULTS: EEAs were performed in 56 (69.1%) and extended EEAs in 25 (30.9%) patients. Intraoperative cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage occurred in 48 cases (59.3%) and was graded as 1 in 12.3%, 2 in 34.6%, and 3 in 12.3%. Reconstruction types 1, 2, and 3 were used in 40.7%, 46.9%, and 12.4% of cases, respectively. Gross total resection was achieved in 72.9%. Postoperative CSF leakage occurred in 2.5%. On exploratory multivariate analysis, reconstruction complexity was independently associated with higher postoperative SNOT-22 score (B = 3.379, 95% CI: 0.827-5.930, P = .010). CONCLUSION: The moSBA appears to be a feasible and safe option for selected sellar and suprasellar lesions, providing favorable surgical and functional outcomes in this single-center experience. Although higher reconstruction complexity was independently associated with higher postoperative SNOT-22 scores, residual confounding related to surgical invasiveness, skull base defect magnitude, and intraoperative CSF leakage severity cannot be excluded.

documents.abstract: The emergence and proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have transformed workplace interactions, reshaping many of them into dense “Prompt-response (P-R)” cycles characterized by a structural imbalance between the effort employees invest in crafting prompts and the quality of AI-generated feedback. While existing GenAI literature has largely focused on the scale, frequency, and operational patterns of its application, it has largely overlooked the inherent imbalances within these P-R cycles. Building on control theory, this study investigates how and when GenAI usage is related to employees’ corner-cutting behavior (CCB). Using a scenario-based experiment and a three-wave field survey, we demonstrate that: (i) performance pressure mediates the nonlinear relationship between GenAI usage and CCB, such that this nonlinear indirect effect shifts from positive to negative as GenAI usage intensifies; (ii) workplace status moderates the inverted U-shaped relationship between GenAI usage and performance pressure. Specifically, high status sharpens this curve, whereas low status flattens it, with a complete reversal to a U-shaped relationship occurring only under conditions of extremely low status. By conceptualizing GenAI usage through the dual lenses of expectation induction and cognitive friction operating within P-R cycles, our findings extend and refine traditional perspectives on human-AI interaction in the workplace.

Artificial intelligence has moved in a few short years from narrow tools to general-purpose systems that write, reason and act. The people building these systems now speak openly of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and, beyond it, Artificial Superintelligence (ASI). This Article traces that evolution, sets out the present and future threats it poses to human beings, and examines how five Indian statutes (the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 and the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023) fall short. It proposes specific amendments to each, along with cross-cutting institutional reforms, so that as machines grow more capable, responsibility and control stay with people.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming an important component of digital transformation in healthcare, with particular potential to improve access to primary medical care. Primary care is the first point of contact between individuals and healthcare systems and plays a fundamental role in prevention, early diagnosis, health monitoring, referral, and continuity of care. However, geographical distance, shortages of healthcare professionals, increasing patient demand, limited diagnostic capacity, and unequal distribution of healthcare resources continue to restrict access to primary medical services. This article examines the role and significance of AI in addressing these barriers and evaluates the principal mechanisms through which AI can improve accessibility, efficiency, continuity, and equity in primary care. A narrative analytical review of scientific literature and international health-policy documents was conducted. Particular attention was given to AI-supported symptom assessment, clinical decision support, risk prediction, automated patient triage, remote monitoring, personalized prevention, administrative automation, and multilingual digital health services. The analysis demonstrates that AI can expand the effective capacity of primary care by supporting healthcare professionals, enabling earlier identification of health risks, reducing unnecessary visits, and facilitating remote access to preliminary medical guidance. At the same time, AI implementation introduces significant challenges related to algorithmic bias, data privacy, cybersecurity, explainability, digital exclusion, clinical responsibility, and unequal technological infrastructure. Therefore, AI should not be regarded as a substitute for primary healthcare professionals but as an augmentative technology integrated into a human-centred primary care model. The study proposes a conceptual framework in which AI improves access through five interconnected mechanisms: availability, affordability, timeliness, geographical reach, and continuity of care. Responsible governance, clinical validation, interoperability, digital literacy, and equitable infrastructure are identified as essential conditions for sustainable implementation.

documents.abstract: In modern education, technology plays an indispensable role, fundamentally reshaping instructional and learning methods across diverse academic fields, particularly within English language teaching. The integration of digital learning technologies provides innovative opportunities to improve students' engagement, motivation, and learning interest. This study aims to explore how English language learning technology enhances students' interest in learning English through a qualitative research approach. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, classroom observations, and document analysis involving English teachers and secondary school students. The findings reveal that technology-based learning environments encourage active participation, foster collaborative learning, increase students' confidence, and provide flexible access to learning resources. Applications such as Google Classroom, Quizizz, Kahoot!, Duolingo, YouTube, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based learning platforms positively influence students' enthusiasm toward English learning by making lessons more interactive and enjoyable. The study concludes that educational technology can substantially improve students' learning interest when integrated with appropriate pedagogical strategies and adequate institutional support. The findings provide valuable insights for educators, policymakers, and curriculum developers seeking to enhance English language education in the digital era

The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed education, from adaptive learning systems and AI-based tutoring assistants to automated assessment. While AI offers unprecedented efficiency and personalization, it simultaneously raises fundamental questions about the nature of knowledge, the role of teachers, and the values embedded in the educational process. This article examines the urgency of philosophy of science as a critical-reflective framework for addressing AI development in education, using a library research approach that reviews relevant academic literature. The findings show that the three main branches of philosophy of science, namely ontology, epistemology, and axiology, can serve as analytical instruments to understand the nature of AI, how AI generates knowledge, and the ethical implications of its use in education. Philosophy of science plays an important role in preventing the reduction of learning into a merely mechanical process while ensuring that technology remains framed by human values. The article concludes that integrating philosophy of science into AI-based education discourse is not merely a theoretical complement but an urgent necessity to keep education humanistic amid technological disruption.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to analyse the scientific production on the use of drones in public safety, identifying patterns of development, collaboration networks, intellectual structure, thematic evolution and research gaps in the field. Design/methodology/approach The research adopts a quantitative, descriptive and exploratory approach based on bibliometric analysis. Data were collected from the Scopus database, covering the period from 2021 to 2025. A total of 361 journal articles were analysed using performance indicators and science mapping techniques. The study employs PyBibX for performance analysis and VOSviewer and Bibliometrix (R) for co-authorship, co-citation, keyword co-occurrence and conceptual structure analysis through Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA). Additionally, a PRISMA-based protocol was applied to identify a core set of 65 articles for thematic classification. Findings The results indicate that research on drones in public safety is a rapidly expanding and highly collaborative field, characterised by strong internationalisation and interdisciplinary integration. The intellectual structure is supported by multiple interconnected domains, including artificial intelligence, signal processing, autonomous systems, and security studies. Thematic analysis reveals that drones function as central elements in the transition towards data-driven policing, enabling real-time monitoring, predictive analytics and operational optimisation. However, the study also identifies significant challenges related to regulatory gaps, cybersecurity risks, institutional barriers and ethical concerns, particularly regarding privacy, legitimacy and social acceptance. Research limitations/implications The study is limited to the Scopus database, English-language journal articles, and the 2021–2025 period, which may exclude relevant contributions from other sources or earlier foundational studies. Future research should incorporate multiple databases, extend temporal coverage, and explore qualitative and empirical approaches, particularly regarding governance, regulation, and societal impacts. Practical implications The findings provide insights for policymakers, public safety agencies, and practitioners by highlighting key applications, technological requirements, and implementation challenges associated with drone adoption. The study supports strategic decision-making related to resource allocation, operational integration, and technological investment in security systems. Social implications The increasing use of drones in public safety has significant implications for the relationship between the state and society, particularly in terms of surveillance, privacy, and institutional trust. The results emphasize the need for transparent governance, procedural justice, and proportional use of technology to ensure social legitimacy and public acceptance. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by providing a comprehensive bibliometric and conceptual mapping of drones in public safety, integrating technological, organizational, and sociotechnical perspectives. It advances the field by proposing an analytical interpretation of UAVs as platforms of datafication, supporting the transition towards data-driven security systems.

Although media literacy interventions are increasingly used to counter misinformation, many remain text-centered and non-interactive, limiting engagement during real-time evaluation. This limitation is particularly consequential for visual misinformation, where realistic synthetic images can encourage intuitive judgments. This study examines how two chatbot design features—interactive evaluation format and chatbot (im)perfection disclosure—shape perceived user and AI agency and, in turn, truth discernment. In an online experiment (N = 348), participants evaluated visual misinformation in a chatbot-supported task varying these two features. Interactive evaluation increased perceived user agency but decreased perceived AI agency, whereas imperfection disclosure modestly increased user agency without affecting AI agency. Critically, interactive evaluation indirectly reduced truth discernment through increased perceived user agency. These findings reveal a potential user agency trap: chatbot interactivity can make users feel more empowered while paradoxically undermining their ability to discern visual misinformation.

Navy divers are essential personnel for the operations of the fleet, supporting underwater ship maintenance, deep-sea salvage, and special naval warfare. Their effectiveness, however, is limited by heat loss in conventional wetsuits. Traditional neoprene wetsuits progressively lose insulating performance at depth because the increasing hydrostatic pressure compresses the neoprene’s closed-cell foam structure. To solve this problem, we developed a series of segmented wetsuits (K-suits) built by enhancing a neoprene undercoat with external pockets containing composite material plates made of incompressible hollow microspheres embedded in silicone. The K-suits significantly outperformed traditional 7 mm neoprene suits in field tests. Herein, we report on improved composites. A combination of 30 elastomers and additives was evaluated using American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM) methods, including thermal conductivity testing (C518-21), compression testing (D575-91), slow-rate penetration testing (F1306-21), and custom impact testing. The results showed that multiple material combinations improve insulation, compressive strength, and resistance to puncture. Among all tested options, Sylgard 527 (S-527) with embedded 3M K1 glass microsphere had the best thermal insulation performance. Furthermore, its high flexibility makes it well suited for use in multilayer K-suits.

Monte Carlo particle transport codes are powerful tools, but their use requires substantial knowledge of input preparation, execution, and result analysis. In this study, we present a code-side strategy for applying existing AI assistants and AI agents to PHITS. Two complementary sets of AI-ready resources were prepared from manuals, lecture materials, sample inputs, utility information, and developer-curated cautions: a bundled knowledge base for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based assistants and a compact agent reference for direct use by AI agents. The knowledge base was loaded into Gemini Notebook to provide conversational PHITS support, while the agent reference was combined with PHITS-specific policies and execution rules to enable AI agents to edit input files, execute calculations, inspect errors, analyze results, and assist with source-code modification and compilation. To evaluate the agent-driven workflow, five demonstration tasks were executed ten times with different AI agents and computing environments. The results showed that AI agents could handle complex PHITS workflows when appropriate resources and rules were provided. Practical lessons included precise prompts, human verification, well-documented sample files, explicit execution policies, and command-line-accessible tools. These findings support bundling AI-ready resources with particle transport codes to enable the use of general-purpose AI tools without requiring dedicated code-specific applications.

Abstract Force field models are one of the central pillars of molecular simulations. A large number of molecular force field models has been developed in the past decades─mostly published in scientific papers. Building machine-readable force field input files for simulation engines is a tedious and error-prone task. We developed a method for extracting and building force field files from publications using large language models (LLMs). We have tested the new method by extracting 114 force field models from 21 scientific publications. The studied force fields comprise 6–74 parameters that were automatically extracted, identified, annotated, and allocated. We have compared the performance of different LLMs, namely Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 4 Sonnet, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and GPT-4o. Overall, they yield similar performance─yet there are important differences in individual cases. The overall best performance was obtained by the Gemini 2.5 Pro LLM. The force field parameters were extracted and identified with an accuracy of 94.0% using the Gemini 2.5 Pro LLM. The new LLM-assisted extraction method drastically reduces the time required for building force field files. Nevertheless, human-in-the-loop verification is still indispensable.

The One Exposome framework integrates exposomics, One Health toxicology, New Approach Methodologies (NAMs) and artificial intelligence to advance environmental health from reactive risk assessment towards predictive, preventive, and participatory science. The paper positions One Health as the ethical and conceptual rationale for recognizing the interdependence of human, animal, and environmental health, the Exposome as the framework for measuring cumulative and life-course exposures, and NAMs together with digital and AI-enabled tools as the means to generate, integrate, and interpret mechanistic and adverse outcome pathway (AOP)-based evidence across biological scales. In this review, environmental health challenges such as antimicrobial resistance, endocrine disruption, and other complex multi-stressor exposures cannot be adequately addressed through compartmentalized, single-substance, or purely retrospective approaches. The One Exposome paradigm instead proposes a systems-based model that links exposure data, mechanistic toxicology, and public health intelligence across humans, animals, and ecosystems. It draws on human-relevant NAMs, including microphysiological systems, together with AI and multi-omics approaches, to support cross-species interpretation, earlier hazard identification, and more preventive intervention strategies. Within this framework, sentinel surveillance, integrated monitoring, and interoperable data systems are central for detecting shared risks across environmental, veterinary, food, and human health domains. The approach is also presented as requiring governance reform so that agricultural practice, environmental management, and clinical stewardship are aligned within a common preventive and planetary health perspective. Overall, the paper frames the One Exposome as a transdisciplinary architecture for environmental public health that combines measurable environments, mechanistic understanding, and computational integration. By connecting cumulative exposures to biological responses and population-level consequences, it offers a foundation for more anticipatory, equitable, and scientifically integrated environmental health decision-making.

Abstract This study reports the AI-assisted transformation of Compound Chain, a validated physical inorganic chemistry card game, into a browser-based learning application. The development used a “vibe coding” approach, in which educators describe functionality in natural language while an LLM generates and refines the code. We propose a five-step Pedagogical System Architect framework, intended for chemistry educators without programming experience, that covers architectural planning, data design, incremental implementation, AI-assisted debugging, and version control. The digital version extends the original game through automated rule enforcement, a zoom interface, and single-player mode, in a manner consistent with reduced extraneous cognitive load, and supporting self-regulated practice beyond class. In an exploratory classroom deployment, voluntary out-of-class usage (a self-reported approximation of 4.5 sessions per student) suggests that the digital format can transform a classroom activity into an intrinsically motivated practice resource. This exploratory evaluation documents engagement, usability, and voluntary practice; establishing conceptual learning gains from the digital version remains a question for future controlled study.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Introduction As generative AI becomes increasingly available in teacher education, a central question is how pre-service teachers interpret, evaluate, and translate different feedback sources into coherent design decisions. This study examined how 22 South Korean pre-service mathematics teachers used AI and peer feedback while revising sustainability-oriented mathematical modeling tasks on school cafeteria food waste, a context aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 12. Methods Using an exploratory, comparative mixed-methods sequence-comparison design embedded in an authentic teacher-education course, participants received two rounds of feedback in different sequences: AI followed by peer feedback or peer feedback followed by AI. Framed within cognitive, affective, and behavioral dimensions of feedback engagement, the analysis combined double-coded ratings of initial and final task designs, feedback-response records, revision-depth coding, validation-focused revision indicators, and post-activity reflections. Results Participants rarely copied feedback passively: 20 selectively accepted feedback in at least one round, and 17 made at least one structural or reconceptual revision. Five participants showed a positive composite gain in rated task-design quality. Participants valued AI feedback for its specificity, new perspectives, and speed, and more often made validation-focused revisions after it, whereas they valued peer feedback for mutual communication, classroom realism, and student perspective. Descriptive comparisons showed different engagement trajectories across the sequence conditions alongside similar composite-quality changes. Discussion Feedback translation provides an analytic perspective on the divergence between revision activity and artifact quality. Within this course context, the findings show how feedback evaluation, revision decisions, and artifact quality can diverge and suggest that teacher educators should scaffold evaluative judgment, source comparison, and post-revision coherence checking.

Narrative gravity is a system-level diagnostic heuristic for explaining why some transmedia storyworlds remain coherent under platform fragmentation while others lose interpretive stability. The problem is not simply how stories circulate or whether a world possesses a stable core. It is what coherence looks like after circulation, when audiences increasingly encounter a world as isolated fragments and sequence cannot reliably do the work of orientation on first contact. This chapter shifts the focus from expansion to what I call the partial-entry problem: the moment coherence must be sustained even when first contact is incomplete. I propose narrative gravity as a heuristic to locate where the work of coherence is actually being carried, whether in texts, paratexts, or community infrastructures. The framework operates across three analytically distinct but systemically linked dimensions: thematic constancy, structural necessity, and ethical resonance. These dimensions work at different analytical scales, narratological, formal, and sociological respectively, but they converge on a shared object: the maintenance infrastructure that keeps a storyworld legible over time. A historical analogue, the Great Siege of Malta, grounds the argument against presentism. The chapter then extends the analysis to feed-based environments and generative AI contexts, introducing Proof of Humanity as a way to track responsibility and trust when provenance becomes unstable.

Large language models now write a substantial share of new source code, yet the mechanisms by which organisations establish confidence in that code have hardly changed. Independent testing indicates that AI-generated code introduces security weaknesses in close to half of evaluated tasks, while European regulation – notably the Cyber Resilience Act and the AI Act – places increasing responsibility on those who place software on the market. This paper argues that the decisive constraint on the productive use of AI in software engineering is no longer the generation of code but its verification. It describes the structural sources of the resulting trust gap, outlines the European regulatory context, and proposes six design principles for a "trust layer" that sits between AI coding agents and production systems. Particular attention is given to small and medium-sized enterprises and to regulated organisations that cannot transfer source code to external cloud services.

topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: This chapter provides a comprehensive review of medical research methods. Both learning paradigms, algorithms, and practical aspects will be explored in depth to reveal their unique features, strengths, and weaknesses. Advanced learning, such as classification and regression, is investigated by their use in disease prediction, diagnostic imaging, and treatment outcome prediction. Unsupervised learning methods (such as clustering algorithms, pattern detection, and healthcare data mining) are tested for the one that is ready to be processed on patient stratification, pattern detection, and healthcare data mining. This chapter compares these methodologies, taking also into account data availability, computational complexity, interpretation, and clinical usability. In addition to clinical problems relating to clinical healthcare applications, mathematical gleanings of critical algorithms are included. Particular attention is being paid to hybrid approaches that combine controlled and unsupervised approaches to health problems. An in-depth review of case studies, success criteria, and validation methods is included in this chapter to demonstrate how both learning paradigms can contribute to healthcare research and improve clinical decision support and personalized medicine. We discuss current trends, limitations, and future directions of research in this area, which may lead to improved machine learning–based healthcare delivery systems.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Xây dựng đề cương học phần theo chuẩn đầu ra cần sự phối hợp giữa chuẩn đầu ra chương trình, học phần với nội dung, hoạt động dạy học và phương pháp đánh giá. Bài báo đề xuất một khung kiến trúc ứng dụng AI nhằm hỗ trợ giảng viên xây dựng và đánh giá đề cương học phần. Nghiên cứu sử dụng phương pháp Design Science Research (DSR), kết hợp nghiên cứu tài liệu, phân tích khái niệm và thiết kế artefact. Cơ sở sư phạm gồm: Constructive Alignment (tính đồng bộ kiến tạo), Backward Design (thiết kế ngược) và Bloom’s Taxonomy (thang đo Bloom) Cơ sở công nghệ gồm mô hình ngôn ngữ lớn (LLM) và Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Khung đề xuất gồm bốn tầng: giao diện, ứng dụng, AI và nghiệp vụ cùng với dữ liệu và tri thức với sáu module từ phân tích chuẩn đầu ra của chương trình đào tạo (Program Learning Outcomes - PLO), tạo chuẩn đầu ra học phần (Course Learning Outcomes - CLO) đến đề xuất dạy học, đánh giá, kiểm tra chất lượng và tổng hợp đề cương. Cơ chế Human-in-the-Loop (mô hình làm việc kết hợp giữa trí tuệ nhân tạo (AI) và con người) quy định AI chỉ tạo đề xuất, còn giảng viên kiểm tra, chỉnh sửa và phê duyệt. Bài báo đề xuất thiết kế kiểm định dựa trên Bloom, PLO-CLO alignment, độ phủ nội dung và tính nhất quán, kết hợp độ đo tự động, đánh giá chuyên gia và khảo sát. Kết quả hiện tại là khung kiến trúc và thiết kế kiểm định.

La investigación describe el uso de herramientas de inteligencia artificial en las actividades académicas de los estudiantes de cuarto año, turno vespertino, de la Carrera de Ciencias de la Comunicación Social de la Universidad Técnica de Oruro, Bolivia. El objetivo fue describir la frecuencia de utilización de estas herramientas, las principales actividades académicas en las que son empleadas y la percepción de los estudiantes s obre su contribución al aprendizaje y a la elaboración de trabajos académicos. El estudio se desarrolló bajo un enfoque cuantitativo, con alcance descriptivo y mediante el método inductivo. La población estuvo conformada por estudiantes de cuarto año del turno vespertino y la muestra estuvo constituida por 35 participantes, seleccionados mediante un muestreo no probabilístico por criterio. La información se recopiló mediante una encuesta aplicada a través de un cuestionario digital. Los resultados muestran que el 100 % de los estudiantes encuestados utiliza herramientas de inteligencia artificial al menos ocasionalmente. La búsqueda de información constituye la principal actividad de uso, con el 77,1 %, seguida de la elaboración de trabajos académicos, con el 62,9 %, y la mejora de la redacción, con el 31,4 %. ChatGPT presenta la mayor frecuencia de utilización, con el 51,4 %. Asimismo, el 71,4 % de los participantes percibe que estas herramientas contribuyen a mejorar su aprendizaje, mientras que el 74,3 % considera que facilitan la realización de trabajos académicos. Se concluye que las herramientas de inteligencia artificial forman parte de las prácticas académicas de los estudiantes estudiados y son utilizadas principalmente como apoyo para la búsqueda de información y la elaboración de trabajos académicos.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Vision-Language Models (VLMs) represent a significant advancement in Multimodal Artificial Intelligence by integrating Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing into a unified framework. These models are capable of understanding visual and textual information simultaneously, enabling intelligent reasoning, image understanding, visual question answering, image captioning, and human-computer interaction. Recent developments in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have further enhanced the capability of AI systems to perform complex multimodal tasks with high accuracy and contextual awareness. This review paper presents a comprehensive study of Vision-Language Models, including their architecture, working principles, training methodologies, and recent advancements. The paper examines popular VLMs such as CLIP, BLIP, LLaVA, GPT-4o, Gemini, and Qwen-VL, along with their applications in healthcare, education, robotics, autonomous systems, and assistive technologies. Furthermore, the study discusses the advantages, limitations, and challenges associated with VLMs, including computational complexity, data requirements, bias, and hallucination issues. Finally, future research directions and emerging trends in multimodal AI are highlighted. [1,2]The review concludes that Vision-Language Models are transforming the field of Artificial Intelligence by enabling machines to understand and interact with the world in a more human-like manner. Keywords: Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), Multimodal Artificial Intelligence, Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing, Deep Learning, Image Understanding, Visual Question Answering, Image Captioning, Human-Computer Interaction, Large Language Models, Multimodal Learning.

Construction workers are frequently exposed to postural ergonomic risks, yet conventional AI-based ergonomic risk assessment (ERA) systems generally provide risk classifications or scores rather than interpretable and interactive explanations. This study investigates whether domain adaptation can improve a generic vision–language model’s ability to identify and explain construction ergonomic risks from images. A dataset with 1900 construction image–text pairs was curated. The domain-adapted model was compared with the baseline model. Performance was evaluated using visual question answering (VQA) accuracy, nine image-captioning metrics, and a blinded human evaluation involving 50 participants with varying levels of ergonomics knowledge. ErgoChat improved performance across the nine caption-evaluation metrics and VQA. In the human evaluation, ErgoChat-generated descriptions were selected as more accurate in 81.69% of comparisons. Limitations include dataset size and class imbalance, potential VLM hallucination, and visual-perception errors. Future research will expand and balance real-site data, evaluate prompt robustness, and strengthen integration with structured ergonomic assessment procedures. The primary contribution is therefore a construction-ergonomics-specific domain-adaptation and evaluation framework that enables interactive VQA and natural-language ergonomic risk reasoning.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) travel selfies have emerged as a novel pre-trip tourism touchpoint, yet their role in shaping user responses remains underexplored. Drawing on three-phase affordance actualization theory, this study aims to examine how GenAI travel selfie affordances are associated with user engagement and visit intention. Design/methodology/approach A three-study mixed-methods design was used, combining 32 photo-elicitation interviews, a survey of 526 users analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) of affordance configurations. Findings Three affordances were identified: visual creation, generative controllability and self-presentation. All three were positively associated with cognitive, affective and behavioral engagement, except for one nonsignificant path. User engagement was positively associated with visit intention. The fsQCA results further indicated that high engagement can be associated with multiple affordance configurations. Practical implications GenAI travel selfies can serve as a soft, user-driven promotional touchpoint for destinations and hospitality brands. Designers and marketers could consider identity-relevant design, controllable and reliable generative functions and visually appealing outputs to encourage engagement and stimulate early-stage destination interest. Originality/value The research is among the early empirical studies of GenAI travel selfies in tourism. It extends affordance-based research to a visual, identity-centered GenAI context and combines net-effect and configurational evidence to explain how these affordances are linked to user engagement and visit intention.

This paper presents a qualitative thematic analysis of in-depth interviews with ten digital media, journalism, and corporate communication professionals, conducted as part of a doctoral study on the transformative effects of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on digital media. Participants included journalists, content creators, software engineers, and communication and partnerships professionals. Using a six-phase thematic analysis approach, five major themes were identified: (1) AI as an efficiency and workflow multiplier; (2) the double-edged relationship between AI and creativity; (3) erosion of authenticity, credibility, and trust; (4) audience personalisation and the surveillance undertone of engagement; and (5) ethical and regulatory anxiety around misinformation, deepfakes, privacy, and job displacement. Across all themes, participants consistently positioned AI as a 'force multiplier for human judgement, not a replacement for it,' emphasising that responsibility for accuracy, editorial judgement, and accountability must remain with human professionals even as routine tasks become increasingly automated. The findings complement a parallel quantitative survey of 300 digital media consumers conducted for the same doctoral project, offering an inside-the-industry perspective on patterns the survey data reveal at the level of public perception.
